plan.summary: The traceAgent span-timing test fails under the full `pnpm test` run but passes alone. The cause is not shared tracer state. Every test builds its own BasicTracerProvider. The test drives a fake clock that starts at 1000 ms, and traceAgent passes each event's `at` to OpenTelemetry as a plain millisecond number. The OpenTelemetry trace SDK reads a number no larger than the process's uptime as time since the process started, not as epoch time. A worker that has been up for less than a second sees the root span start at [1, 0]. A busy worker that has been up longer gets a start time shifted onto the wall clock. The same thing happens to any `@kamp-us/tea` user who runs an agent with a pinned or replayed clock. After the fix, the spans traceAgent and agentSpans export carry exactly the `at` of the transitions that opened and closed them, whatever the process uptime. The test is then deterministic under any load.

stories.want: the otel span-timing test to pass or fail the same way whether its file runs alone or in the full suite
stories.why: so unrelated PRs don't go red and spend repair rounds on a test they never touched

stories.who: a developer using `@kamp-us/tea`'s traceAgent or agentSpans with an injected clock (a pinned test clock or a replayed run)
stories.want: exported spans to start and end at exactly the `at` of the transitions that opened and closed them
stories.why: so the trace shows the run's real timeline instead of times that depend on how long the process has been up

pointers.why: The failing test. The fake clock starts at 1000 (line 110), and the test asserts `root.startTime` equals [1, 0].

Each `startTime: at` and `span.end(at)` passes a bare ms number to OTel. Converting `at` to an HrTime tuple (or a Date) there avoids the SDK's guess that a number is relative to process start. Lines 280/283 call `end()` with no time on detach; leave those alone.

The SDK rule behind the bug: a number input that is ≤ otperformance.now() becomes hrTime(inp + performanceOffset). HrTime and Date inputs skip this rule. Not vendored here (no node_modules in the snapshot), so check it in the installed version. A test can force the condition by stubbing performance.now to return a large value.
Shows each test builds its own provider and exporter, which rules out a shared global tracer provider.
@kamp-us/tea is published, and fixing span times for users on an injected clock is a user-visible fix.

questions.ask: Should this fix traceAgent and agentSpans themselves, or only make the test use epoch-scale clock values?
options: Fix the library: pass `at` to OpenTelemetry in a form it can't misread, so users on pinned or replayed clocks get exact span times
Fix only the test: start the fake clock at an epoch-scale value (e.g. Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1)) and leave the library alone
questions.why: The flaky test is a symptom of a real library bug. Any `@kamp-us/tea` user who injects a small clock (tests, replay) gets span times that silently depend on process uptime. Fixing the test alone would hide that bug. The job criterion and the agentSpans small-`at` criterion depend on this lean. Under the test-only option, only the `pnpm test` criterion remains.

plan.summary: `code-graph --boundaries` only checks an import when the importing file is inside a declared feature (B1/B2) or in a `lib` folder (B3). Every other file is skipped. So while a repo is adopting one feature at a time, most of its code can import a feature's internals and `--boundaries --ci` stays green. After this change, a new rule B4 flags any import from a file outside every declared feature and outside `lib` that reaches a feature anywhere other than its index.ts. B4 violations count toward the same per-scope ceiling in `boundary-ceilings.json`, so existing debt can be recorded and then ratcheted down.

stories.why: declaring a feature actually walls it off on day one, not only against other declared features

stories.want: today's outside-to-internal imports counted under the same per-scope ceiling, recordable with `--write-ceilings` and failing on EXCEEDED or SLACK
stories.why: existing debt can be frozen and paid down without blocking the switch-on, and new leaks fail the build

stories.who: someone reading `--boundaries` output, its `--json` form, the README or the `--help` text
stories.want: the new rule shown and documented as B4, next to B1–B3
stories.why: they can tell why an edge was flagged and how to fix it (import through the feature's index.ts)

plan.summary: Today a `--layers` path pattern can only be a path prefix, and `*` only works as a whole segment. A pattern like `**/*-plumbing.ts` matches nothing, so a repo that marks a module's role in its filename can't declare those roles as layers. After this change, `**` matches zero or more folders and `*` inside a segment matches part of a name (never crossing `/`), so filename-role layers claim their files at any depth. Plain prefixes work exactly as before, and when two patterns claim the same file, the more specific one wins or the gate refuses the tie with a clear message. The README documents both new forms.

stories.why: so the layer gate, with its allowlist ratchet, unlayered census and per-site lines, enforces "business rules never import plumbing" and the rule doesn't have to fall back to an ast-grep check

stories.who: someone whose existing `--layer-rules` file uses only prefixes and whole-segment `*`
stories.want: their layers to classify every file exactly as they did before
stories.why: so upgrading doesn't silently move files between layers and break their allowlist

stories.who: someone writing a rules file that mixes directory-prefix layers and filename-role layers that can claim the same file
stories.want: to know which layer wins, and to be stopped when two layers' patterns are equally specific
stories.why: so a file's layer is never decided by an accident of pattern order

stories.want: to see `**` and in-segment `*` documented next to `*`, along with how specificity treats them

questions.ask: Should a tie between layers be refused when the rules file loads, from the patterns alone, or when a run actually finds a file that two tied patterns from different layers both claim?
options: Refuse at load: any two patterns from different layers with equal specificity
Refuse at run time: only when one file is actually claimed by two tied patterns from different layers, naming the file
Don't refuse; keep a deterministic tiebreak such as declaration order
questions.why: Whether two globs overlap can't be decided cheaply from the patterns, and a load-time rule would refuse harmless pairs: `services` and `packages` tie on depth, segments and characters (8 each) yet never claim the same file. The tie-refusal criterion and the README tie criterion depend on this.

questions.ask: When a directory-prefix layer (e.g. `services`) and a filename-role layer (e.g. `**/*-plumbing.ts`) both claim `services/billing/billing-plumbing.ts`, which should win?
options: Keep the current order (depth, then whole literal segments) and only add literal characters as a final tiebreak; `**` adds no depth
Rank by literal characters first, so the role pattern usually wins over a short prefix
Always let a pattern that reaches the filename beat a prefix that only claims a folder
questions.lean: Keep the current order and add literal characters only as the last tiebreak.
questions.why: Ranking by characters first would reorder existing prefix-only configs: `services/*/src` (depth 3) currently beats `services/billing` (depth 2), but `services/billing` has more literal characters. plan.summary: Today `readAllowance` excuses B8 only when the driving file also imports, at runtime, a library of a `decidedBy` type. A thin read handler that decides nothing (it parses input, calls one listed driven read file and returns the answer) therefore stays B8 forever. After this change `decidedBy` can be left out of a scope's allowance. With it left out, any driving file that imports a listed read-only driven file is excused, and a listed file with a `write` data site still voids the allowance.
